title: Rewrite Your LinkedIn 'About' Section That Actually Gets Read
expectedOutcome:
**Version 1 — Direct**
I rebuilt onboarding at Acme so 60% of new accounts hit their first 'aha moment' in under 3 minutes — up from 22%.

I'm a product designer who thinks in numbers. Five years at B2B SaaS taught me that a 'beautiful' flow is meaningless if the activation rate didn't move. I care about the click-by-click reality of how strangers learn your product, and I'm allergic to design that wins awards but loses retention.

I'm now looking for a senior IC or design lead role at a Series A-C product company that takes activation seriously. Bonus points if you're in fintech or developer tools.

DMs are open if you want to talk about onboarding, activation math, or design hiring.

---

**Version 2 — Story-driven**
My first product job, I shipped a beautiful onboarding flow. Activation dropped 8%. That week taught me more than design school did.

Five years later, I think about activation the way engineers think about latency — as a moral obligation. At Acme I rebuilt onboarding around a single rule: every screen has to earn its place. New-account 'aha' jumped from 22% to 60%.

I'm hunting for a senior design role where the team treats activation as a craft, not a funnel chart. Series A through C, fintech or dev tools especially.

If you're hiring or just want to swap notes on activation work, my DMs are open.
tips: Be aggressive on the numbers — vague claims kill this prompt. If you don't have hard metrics, give qualitative wins ('rewrote the docs site that PMs at 4 different teams now reference').

title: LinkedIn Headline That Gets Profile Views
expectedOutcome:
1. Senior Product Designer | B2B SaaS Activation & Onboarding
   → Pure keyword play. Recruiters searching exact terms find you first.

2. Senior Product Designer · Helped Acme 3x activation rate in 6 months
   → Adds a credibility number without sounding boastful.

3. Designing onboarding for B2B SaaS · ex-Acme, ex-Linear
   → Lets brand names do the work; great if your past companies are recognizable.

4. Senior Product Designer | Activation > pixels | Writing weekly about onboarding metrics
   → Signals you have an opinion + content presence. Filters for the right roles.

5. Product Designer turning 'looks great' onboarding into 'works great' onboarding
   → Story-shaped. Stops the scroll on the search results page.

6. I rebuild onboarding flows for B2B SaaS so activation rates move 30%+
   → Plain-English value prop. Skips the title entirely (works because they see your job below).

7. Senior Product Designer | If your activation rate is below 40%, we should talk.
   → CTA-in-the-headline. Risky but extremely high response rate.

8. Closing the gap between 'beautiful' design and 'activated' users · Sr. Designer at Acme
   → Frames your point of view as a problem statement.

9. Activation, onboarding, & the boring math behind great B2B SaaS UX
   → Topic-first headline. Great if you're building a content audience.

10. I think activation rate is the only design metric that matters. I might be wrong.
   → Contrarian + humble. Extremely scroll-stopping but only works if your content backs it up.
tips: Test the headline by searching LinkedIn for your target keywords from another account — if your profile doesn't surface in the top 20, the headline isn't keyword-loaded enough.

title: Ask for a LinkedIn Recommendation Without Feeling Awkward
expectedOutcome:
Hey Priya,

I was just walking someone through how we landed the Nordstrom pilot last year and remembered you basically saved that pitch — the way you reframed the data midway through the call still gets quoted on my team.

If you're up for it, would you mind dropping a short LinkedIn recommendation? I'm updating my profile for a few senior PM conversations and the ones I'm proudest of are things we built together. Specifically, I'd love it if you touched on how I work cross-functionally with engineering on ambiguous problems — that's the thread I'm trying to make stand out.

Happy to write a rough draft so you only have to tweak/sign off — let me know which is easier.

No rush. Owe you a coffee either way.

- Maya
tips: Always offer to write the draft for them. People say yes 2-3x more often when the friction is 'review and edit' vs 'write from scratch'.

title: Write a LinkedIn Recommendation That Actually Sounds Like You
expectedOutcome:
I remember the first time Daniel pushed back on me in a planning meeting. I was wrong, the data was on his side, and he made the case without making me feel cornered. That moment told me everything about how he works.

title: Optimize Your CV/Resume for ATS Filters Without Killing the Tone
promptText:
I'm submitting my resume to a company that uses an ATS (applicant tracking system). Optimize my resume bullets so they survive keyword filters while still reading like a human wrote them.

ROLE I'M APPLYING FOR: {role_title_and_company}
JOB DESCRIPTION I'M TARGETING: {paste_the_full_job_description}

MY CURRENT BULLETS (paste 5-10 bullets):
```
{paste_your_bullets}
```

DO:
1. Extract the 10 most important keywords/phrases from the job description (skills, tools, methodologies).
2. Rewrite each of my bullets to include 1-2 of those keywords naturally — not stuffed.
3. Keep every bullet under 2 lines. Start with a strong verb. Quantify outcomes where possible.
4. Preserve specific numbers and proper nouns I gave you. Don't invent achievements.
5. Output as a table: 'Original | Optimized | Keywords inserted'

DO NOT:
- Add fake metrics.
- Use buzzwords (synergize, leverage, spearhead, drive, dynamic).
- Lose information I included.
expectedOutcome:
**Top keywords from JD:** Python, Snowflake, dbt, A/B testing, data modeling, stakeholder communication, experimentation, BigQuery, dashboarding, SQL optimization

| Original | Optimized | Keywords inserted |
|---|---|---|
| Built data pipelines for marketing team | Designed Python + dbt pipelines feeding Snowflake that cut marketing's daily reporting lag from 6h to under 30 min | Python, dbt, Snowflake |
| Helped with A/B testing for the team | Owned experimentation framework for 4 product squads — defined success metrics, ran SQL analysis on 30+ A/B tests/quarter | A/B testing, SQL, experimentation |
| Made dashboards for execs | Built and maintained 12 executive dashboards in Looker, reducing ad-hoc data requests by ~40% per quarter | Dashboarding |
| Worked with engineering on data infra | Partnered with engineering to migrate 200+ legacy queries from Redshift to BigQuery; cut warehouse spend 35% | BigQuery, data modeling |
| Trained junior analysts | Onboarded 3 junior analysts on our SQL style guide and dbt patterns; all 3 are now shipping models independently | dbt, SQL optimization, stakeholder communication |
tips: Paste the FULL job description — keywords get extracted from the qualifications + responsibilities sections specifically. Don't optimize for keywords that aren't in your actual experience; ATS catches stuffing.

title: Build STAR-Format Interview Stories From Your Real Work
promptText:
Help me build 5 polished interview stories using the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) from the raw notes below. These need to be ready to say out loud in 2-3 minutes each.

ROLE I'M INTERVIEWING FOR: {role_title}
THE 5 BEHAVIORAL QUESTIONS I'M PREPARING FOR: {list_the_5_questions}

RAW NOTES — projects, conflicts, wins, failures from my actual work (be messy, don't pre-edit):
```
{paste_your_notes}
```

FOR EACH QUESTION:
1. Pick the single best project from my notes that maps to that question.
2. Build a STAR story: Situation (1-2 sentences setting context), Task (your specific responsibility), Action (3-5 concrete things YOU did — not 'we'), Result (quantified outcome + what you'd do differently).
3. Each story should be ~250 words when said out loud (90-120 seconds).
4. Flag any story where the 'Result' is weak — tell me what to ask my former teammates to strengthen it.

Do NOT invent details. If my notes are thin somewhere, ask me a specific clarifying question instead of making things up.
expectedOutcome:
**Q1: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager**

*Situation:* In Q2 2024, my manager wanted us to ship a new pricing page in 3 weeks to hit a board commitment.

*Task:* I was the design lead and believed shipping in 3 weeks would land a worse experience than our current page — which would tank conversion right when the board was watching.

*Action:* (1) I built a quick conversion-impact model showing the likely 8-15% drop. (2) Booked a 30-min meeting with my manager and the head of growth specifically to walk through the model. (3) Proposed a 2-week alternative: ship a copy refresh + pricing table to old layout, get conversion learnings, then redesign in Q3. (4) Owned the conversation, didn't escalate over their head. (5) When they ultimately agreed, I made sure to credit my manager publicly for greenlighting the shift.

*Result:* We shipped the copy refresh in 11 days. Conversion went up 6%, not down. Q3 redesign launched on schedule with much better data behind it.

*What I'd do differently:* I waited 2 days before bringing the disagreement up. I should have raised it the same hour I had the concern.

---

**Q2: ... (similar structure)**

**Weak-result flags:**
- Story 3 (cross-functional conflict): you don't have the final percentage gain. Ask Sam for the Q4 metrics deck — slide 14 should have it.
tips: Practice each story OUT LOUD with a timer. If it goes over 3 minutes, cut the Situation in half. Interviewers tune out at 90 seconds.

title: Tinder/Hinge Bio That Actually Starts Conversations
promptText:
Rewrite my dating app bio so it's specific enough to start a real conversation, not just collect right-swipes.

ABOUT ME (be honest, weird is fine): {your_actual_quirks_jobs_hobbies}
WHAT YOU'RE LOOKING FOR (vibe, not 'long-term partner'): {what_kind_of_person_or_energy}
WHAT YOU DEFINITELY DON'T WANT in messages: {dealbreakers — e.g. 'hey' as a first message}
APP: {Tinder / Hinge / Bumble / etc.}
LENGTH LIMIT: {character_limit_for_that_app}

GOAL: make it specific enough that 70% of replies reference something concrete from the bio.

DO:
- Use 1-2 unusual nouns (not 'food', say 'lemon tarts'; not 'travel', say 'overnight trains').
- Include one tiny invitation — 'tell me your hottest take on X', 'message me only if you've actually read Y'.
- 1 humble brag is OK if it's funny.
- Sound like you talk, not like a corporate bio.

DON'T:
- 'Looking for my partner in crime', 'just ask', 'I take life seriously but not too seriously'.
- Lists of cliches: hiking, sushi, dogs, traveling.
- Anything that sounds like it could be on 1000 other bios.

Give me 3 versions. Tell me which one you'd swipe right on and why.
expectedOutcome:
**Version 1 — Specific & quirky**
Product designer in Berlin who collects old metro maps and is mildly obsessed with the Lisbon yellow tram. Cook badly, ferment things on purpose. Looking for someone who has strong opinions about how to load a dishwasher.

Message me about: bread you've made, songs you put on a 'driving at night' playlist, why your favorite chair is your favorite chair.

Don't message me with 'hey'.

---

**Version 2 — Story-shaped**
Moved to Berlin three years ago for a 6-month contract. Still here. Currently learning to roast my own coffee badly, write better fiction slowly, and play piano never. If you have a strong opinion about an obscure film nobody saw, I want to hear it.

---

**Version 3 — Direct**
Product designer, mid-30s, in Berlin. Climbing 2x a week, slow runs on Sundays, and I read more than I should admit.

Looking for someone who can sit in silence comfortably and also argue about a single book for 2 hours.

First-message bar: tell me a song you've played 100 times this year.

---

**I'd swipe Version 1.** It has the most specific nouns (yellow tram, fermentation, dishwasher opinions) and gives the other person three different conversation entry points instead of one. Specificity is what kills the 'hey' problem.
tips: If you're getting matches but no replies, the bio is the problem. Specificity > cleverness — one weird specific noun beats five witty lines.

title: Wedding Speech That's Funny Without Being Cringe
expectedOutcome:
**Speech (~4 minutes when read aloud):**

[Open] Before I start — yes, I know I'm tall, no, I don't play basketball, please stop asking me at the bar. I'm Maya. I've known Aanya since we were both 19 and we both bought the exact same secondhand couch from the exact same Craigslist guy in the same week. We've been laughing about it for 12 years and we still don't know how it happened.

[Specific anecdote] Aanya is the kind of friend who, when you call her at 2am and say 'I think I made a huge mistake', will ask exactly one question before she's already in an Uber. The huge mistake, by the way, was once that I'd dyed my hair pink during a breakup. She still made it to my apartment in 14 minutes. With a bottle of wine. Pre-judged.

[Pivot to partner — warmly specific] So when she introduced me to Vikram I was prepared to be skeptical. Aanya's threshold for nonsense is famously low. And then I watched him casually fix our broken thermostat at brunch in 4 minutes while quietly arguing with her about whether spiders have feelings. That was the moment I understood. He doesn't slow her down. He gives her room to be more of herself.

[Funny but warm — about the couple] You know what I love about these two? They are the only couple I know where one of them keeps a spreadsheet of which mug is whose, and the other one regularly puts that mug on a high shelf to mess with the spreadsheet. That's marriage. That's the whole thing.

[Land] Aanya, you have made my life louder, weirder, and a thousand times better. Vikram, thank you for marrying my best friend. And for putting up with the spreadsheet.

[Toast] To Aanya and Vikram — may you always have something stupid to argue about and someone to laugh about it with. Cheers.

---

**Why this works:**
- The open is self-deprecating about Maya, not about marriage cliches.
- The 2am story is specific (pink hair, 14 minutes, pre-judged bottle of wine) — generic friendship moments don't land.
- Vikram's intro paragraph uses a tiny specific detail (thermostat + spider argument) instead of 'he's such a great guy'.
- The 'spreadsheet of mugs' beat is the only joke about marriage, and it's earned because it's specific to them.
- Final toast line returns to the opening tone — light, not preachy.
tips: Read it out loud 3 times. If you tear up at the same line you wrote, it'll land. If you don't, the emotional beat is too abstract — make it more specific.

title: 10 YouTube Title Variants Ranked by Click-Through Strategy
promptText:
Generate 10 YouTube title variants for my video, each using a different proven CTR pattern.

VIDEO TOPIC (be detailed): {what_the_video_is_actually_about}
TARGET AUDIENCE: {who_is_this_for}
MY CHANNEL'S NORMAL TONE: {tone — e.g. 'tutorial', 'investigative essay', 'casual founder'}
KEYWORDS YOU'D EXPECT VIEWERS TO SEARCH: {2-4_keywords}
VIDEO LENGTH: {duration}

Use these 10 patterns, one title per pattern. Label each:
1. Plain question hook ('Why does X actually happen?')
2. Specific number + result ('I tried X for 30 days. Here's what changed.')
3. Contrarian POV ('You're wrong about X. Here's why.')
4. Story open ('How I lost X by doing Y')
5. Comparison ('X vs Y after 6 months — which won?')
6. Tutorial direct ('How to X in 10 minutes (no fluff)')
7. Curiosity gap ('Nobody talks about X. They should.')
8. Mistake-prevention ('5 X mistakes that cost me Y')
9. Reaction / opinion ('I watched every X video. They're all wrong about Z.')
10. Authority drop ('A 10-year X explains Y in 8 minutes')

RULES:
- Each title ≤60 chars (YouTube truncates after that on mobile).
- Front-load the keyword in 8 of 10 (skip for hook-style only).
- No clickbait that overpromises. The video must deliver.
- After all 10, recommend the top 3 for THIS specific topic and explain why.
expectedOutcome:
**Video topic: 'How I cut my AWS bill by 60% in a weekend'**

1. **(Question)** Why is your AWS bill 3x bigger than it should be?
2. **(Number/Result)** I cut my AWS bill 60% in one weekend. Here's how.
3. **(Contrarian)** Most AWS cost guides are wrong. Do these 4 things instead.
4. **(Story open)** I almost shut down my SaaS over AWS bills. Then I tried this.
5. **(Comparison)** AWS Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances — what I learned $30k late
6. **(Tutorial direct)** How to audit your AWS bill in 30 minutes (no consultants)
7. **(Curiosity gap)** Nobody is auditing this AWS line item. It's bleeding you.
8. **(Mistake-prevention)** 7 AWS billing mistakes I made so you don't have to
9. **(Reaction/opinion)** I watched every AWS cost video. They miss the point.
10. **(Authority)** A senior cloud architect cuts AWS bills in 8 minutes

---

**Top 3 picks for THIS topic:**
1. **#2 — 'I cut my AWS bill 60% in one weekend. Here's how.'** Specific number, specific time, promise of method. This format wins for technical how-to.
2. **#4 — 'I almost shut down my SaaS over AWS bills. Then I tried this.'** Story open creates higher retention if you actually open with the story. Works best if your normal style is narrative.
3. **#6 — 'How to audit your AWS bill in 30 minutes (no consultants)'** Plain tutorial title with the 'no consultants' parenthetical doing the differentiation work. Best for steady, evergreen traffic.

**Avoid #3 and #9** for this topic — your audience is technical and reacts poorly to 'everyone is wrong' framing unless you have a clear contrarian thesis they can debate.
tips: Pair the chosen title with a thumbnail concept. The best YouTube titles + thumbnails work together — the title raises a question, the thumbnail hints at the answer (or shock).

title: Thumbnail Text Options That Boost CTR Without Looking Like Clickbait
expectedOutcome:
**Title: 'I cut my AWS bill 60% in one weekend. Here's how.'**

1. **$30K WASTED**
   → Shocking-number frame. Hint at the lesson without giving away the method.
2. **NOT WHAT YOU THINK**
   → Contradicts the title's straightforward framing — opens a curiosity gap.
3. **2 NIGHTS, 60%**
   → Doubles down on the speed/result combo from the title.
4. **FREE AUDIT INSIDE**
   → Implies a tool/freebie in the video. High CTR if true.
5. **STOP DOING THIS**
   → Universal stop-doing framing. Pairs with a red strikethrough graphic.
6. **AWS LIED**
   → Provocative authority-flip. Risky but extremely high CTR.
7. **CHECK LINE 47**
   → Mysterious specific number. Forces a click.
8. **WORTH $30K**
   → Frames the video as the payoff, not the lesson.

---

**Best pairing for this title: #3 — '2 NIGHTS, 60%'**
Reinforces the title's specificity (the 'weekend' from the title) while adding a number (60%) that the title also has — repetition + reinforcement increases recall.

**Visual cue:** show your AWS cost graph behind you with a steep drop highlighted in red. Don't put '60%' twice if it's already on the graph — the eye reads the most-prominent number first.
tips: Test 2-3 thumbnails using YouTube's A/B Test feature (now built into Studio). The data is more reliable than your intuition.

title: Instagram Caption That Stops the Scroll With a Story
expectedOutcome:
I lost a $40K client last year because I sent them a Loom video at 11pm.

Not because the work was bad.

Not because the timeline slipped.

Because the Loom video showed me eating dinner in the background.

They didn't say it out loud. They just stopped responding for 6 days, then ghosted.

I used to think 'professionalism' was an old-school idea — that the work was what mattered, not the trappings.

It turns out the trappings are PART of the work. Clients are buying confidence. The Loom in the background was telling them: this person is winging it.

Now I have a 5-minute pre-send checklist: lighting, audio, background, camera height, framing. Took me 3 hours to set up. Costs me 30 seconds per video.

No client has ghosted since.

If you're sending client videos from your kitchen, this is your sign to fix the kitchen.

What's the small thing that quietly killed a deal for you? DM me — collecting these for a piece.

#freelancelife #clientwork #consulting #remotework
tips: Save this caption format and reuse it — the hook style works for any niche. The key is the SPECIFIC number ($40K) and SPECIFIC reason (eating dinner) in the first 4 lines. Generic versions of this caption die at 20 likes.

title: 10-Slide Instagram Carousel That Drives Saves
promptText:
Build a 10-slide Instagram carousel for my topic. Each slide should have specific copy I can drop into Canva/Figma.

TOPIC / TEACH POINT: {what_you_want_to_teach}
MY NICHE: {niche}
MY AUDIENCE'S PAIN: {their_problem}
MY EXPERTISE / WHY ME: {your_credibility_in_one_line}
DESIRED CTA on slide 10: {save? DM? link in bio?}

SLIDE STRUCTURE (write each slide as: 'SLIDE N — [Visual idea] — [Text on slide, max 12 words]'):

1. **Hook slide.** A bold claim or specific number. Stop the scroll. Big text only.
2. **'You vs reality' slide.** Make them realize they have the problem.
3. **'Why this happens' slide.** The misdiagnosis most people make.
4. **The reframe.** The new way to see the problem.
5-8. **The actual steps / framework / tactic** — 1 step per slide, 1 number per slide, 2-line max.
9. **The example or proof.** A 1-line case study or before/after.
10. **CTA slide.** Direct, specific.

RULES:
- Slide 1 must work as a thumbnail (you can't see slide 2+ until they swipe).
- Every slide must be readable in <2 seconds.
- Slide 10's CTA must be specific ('save this for next week' beats 'follow for more').
- Add a brief caption (~80 words) to post alongside that summarizes WHY this matters.
expectedOutcome:
**Topic: 'How to write better cold emails'**

**Slide 1** — [Big text, plain bg] — Your cold emails are bad. It's not the subject line.

**Slide 2** — [Phone mockup of an unread email] — If your reply rate is under 5%, the problem is what's INSIDE the email.

**Slide 3** — [Crossed-out subject line] — Everyone obsesses over subject lines. Subject lines get the OPEN. Bodies get the REPLY.

**Slide 4** — [Two-column compare] — Bad: 'I help companies grow.' Good: 'I noticed your homepage doesn't load on mobile in India.'

**Slide 5** — [Number 1 huge] — Reference something specific from THEIR world. Don't generalize.

**Slide 6** — [Number 2 huge] — Lead with a one-sentence diagnosis, not a one-sentence pitch.

**Slide 7** — [Number 3 huge] — Ask one specific question. Not 'happy to chat'.

**Slide 8** — [Number 4 huge] — Sign off in 4 words. 'Open to a quick call?' beats a paragraph of credentials.

**Slide 9** — [Before/after stat] — Old template: 2% reply rate. New template: 27%. Same audience.

**Slide 10** — [Plain bg, single line] — Save this. Try it on your next 10 cold emails. DM me the results.

---

**Caption to post alongside:**
Cold email reply rates aren't about clever subject lines — they're about whether the recipient feels SEEN in the first 2 lines.

I used to spend hours A/B testing 'Re: quick question' vs '{firstname}, 2-min favour?'

The winning move turned out to be writing one specific sentence about THEM. Reply rates went from 2% to 27% on the same list.

Saving this carousel and trying it on your next batch.

What's the highest reply rate you've ever hit on a cold campaign? DM me.
tips: Slide 1 is doing 80% of the work. If it doesn't stop the scroll, slide 2-10 won't get seen. Make it bold, contrarian, or impossibly specific.

title: 30-Second TikTok Script That Hits in the First 2 Seconds
promptText:
Write a 30-second TikTok script with a hook that lands in the first 2 seconds and a payoff that earns the share.

TOPIC: {what_you_want_to_share}
MY NICHE: {niche}
FORMAT: {talking_head / pov / voiceover / text_overlay / duet}
CALL TO ACTION (optional): {follow? save? part 2?}

SCRIPT STRUCTURE (label each beat with timing):

**0:00-0:02 (hook):** ≤10 words. Must do ONE of:
- Drop a number ('I made $4,200 in 8 days doing this')
- Drop a shocking line ('Your résumé is killing your job search')
- Visual surprise ('Watch what happens when I...')
- Direct address to your viewer ('If you're a [niche], stop doing this NOW.')

**0:02-0:08 (lower the floor):** Make them realize they have the problem too.

**0:08-0:24 (the meat):** 2-3 specific points or steps. NO filler. Each beat = 1 sentence, 1 thing.

**0:24-0:30 (payoff + CTA):** The 'aha' line + a single direct CTA.

RULES:
- Total word count: 70-90 words (about 30 seconds spoken).
- Cuts happen every 2-3 seconds. Mark each [CUT] in the script.
- Include B-roll suggestions in [brackets].
- Don't use 'follow for part 2' unless there's literally a part 2 worth making.
- Sound natural, not scripted. Contractions, fragments, OK.
expectedOutcome:
**Topic: 'Why most people's LinkedIn About section sucks'**

[0:00-0:02 — talking head, sharp cut from black]
"Your LinkedIn About section is doing the OPPOSITE of what you think."

[CUT to phone scrolling through generic About sections]

[0:02-0:08]
"If yours starts with 'I am a passionate, results-driven...' — congratulations, you sound like 90% of people on this app."

[CUT back to talking head, gesture]

[0:08-0:14]
"Recruiters spend 6 seconds. They don't read. They scan for ONE thing: 'is this person specific?'"

[CUT to highlighted bullet on screen: 'BE SPECIFIC']

[0:14-0:24]
"Instead of 'experienced product designer' write 'I rebuilt onboarding at Acme so 60% of new users hit their aha moment in 3 minutes.' One concrete sentence beats three vague ones."

[CUT to before/after of an About section, red strikethroughs]

[0:24-0:30]
"Open your LinkedIn. Read your first sentence. If it could have been written about ANYONE in your industry — rewrite it tonight."

[CUT to text overlay: 'Comment your industry, I'll roast your first line']

**Word count: 86 words.**
tips: Record the hook 3 different ways — different intonation, different first word. Even small delivery changes on the first 2 seconds can 2-3x retention.

title: Storyboard a Sequence of AI-Generated Video Shots (Runway, Pika, Sora)
expectedOutcome:
**Story: 'A woman wakes up alone in a hotel room that's slowly filling with seawater.'**

**MOOD:** Cinematic surreal, blue/grey, soft and unhurried.
**LENGTH:** 30 seconds.
**TOOL:** Runway Gen-3.
**ASPECT:** 16:9.
**REFERENCE:** Tarkovsky pacing, Edward Hopper color.

**Continuity carried across all shots:** A woman, mid-30s, dark wavy hair past shoulders, oversized white linen shirt, no jewelry. Hotel room is muted teal walls, cream curtains, single bed with rumpled grey sheets, an old wood-frame window. Light source is consistently overcast morning, coming from screen-right.

---

**Shot 1 — 3s. Establishing.**
*Visual:* Pull back from window. Empty hotel room, soft morning light. No motion yet.
*Camera:* Static, slight slow zoom out, 35mm equivalent.
*Prompt:* `Wide static shot of a 1970s hotel room interior, muted teal walls, cream curtains slightly moving in still air, single bed with rumpled grey sheets, soft overcast morning light from a wood-frame window on the right, 35mm cinematic, slow gentle zoom out, no people in frame, eerie quiet stillness.`

---

**Shot 2 — 3s. Subject reveal.**
*Visual:* Close-up on the woman's face, eyes opening slowly.
*Camera:* Tight on face, 85mm, very shallow focus.
*Prompt:* `Extreme close-up of a woman with dark wavy shoulder-length hair, mid-30s, lying on a pillow, eyes slowly opening, soft overcast morning light from screen-right, shallow depth of field, cinematic Tarkovsky color grade, muted teal walls slightly out of focus, 85mm lens, slow subtle breath.`

---

**Shot 3 — 3s. Detail insert (the first cue).**
*Visual:* Her hand dangles off the bed. A single drop falls — she pauses.
*Camera:* Side-on detail shot, 50mm.
*Prompt:* `Detail shot of a woman's hand hanging off the edge of an unmade bed in a hotel room, water dripping from her fingertips onto the wooden floor, muted teal wall background, soft overcast morning light, 50mm lens, shallow depth, slow gentle motion.`

---

**Shot 4 — 4s. Wider — water visible on floor.**
*Visual:* The woman sits up. Thin film of seawater across the hotel floor.
*Camera:* Wide low-angle, 24mm, slow dolly toward her.
*Prompt:* `Wide low-angle shot of a woman in an oversized white linen shirt sitting up on the edge of a hotel bed, dark wavy shoulder-length hair, thin film of seawater across the wood floor reflecting the cream curtains and overcast morning light, muted teal walls, slow dolly forward, 24mm cinematic, Edward Hopper color palette.`

---

**Shot 5 — 4s. Tightening.**
*Visual:* Close on her face — she looks down at the water, doesn't move.
*Camera:* 50mm, slow push-in.
*Prompt:* `Close-up of a woman with dark wavy shoulder-length hair in an oversized white linen shirt looking down with a calm, unsurprised expression, soft overcast morning light from screen-right, muted teal hotel wall background, 50mm cinematic, slow push-in, shallow focus, Tarkovsky pacing.`

---

**Shot 6 — 4s. Water rising — wider.**
*Visual:* Water now mid-shin. She stands. Curtains move slightly.
*Camera:* Side-on wide, 35mm, static.
*Prompt:* `Static side-on wide shot of a hotel room interior with seawater rising to mid-shin level, a woman in an oversized white linen shirt standing on the bed, dark wavy hair, cream curtains gently moving, soft overcast morning light, muted teal walls, reflections in the rising water, cinematic 35mm, Edward Hopper color grade.`

---

**Shot 7 — 3s. Detail — the window.**
*Visual:* The window. Outside is more seawater. No city.
*Camera:* Looking outward through the window, 50mm.
*Prompt:* `Looking out a wood-frame hotel window, cream curtains parted slightly, outside is a vast still seawater horizon, no city or land visible, soft overcast morning light, muted blue-grey color palette, 50mm cinematic, very slow gentle motion of the curtains, Tarkovsky atmosphere.`

---

**Shot 8 — 4s. Closing — image, no exposition.**
*Visual:* The woman walks into the water, calmly, until her shoulders are level. She doesn't look back.
*Camera:* Wide rear-three-quarter, 35mm, very slow truck out.
*Prompt:* `Wide rear-three-quarter shot of a woman with dark wavy shoulder-length hair in an oversized white linen shirt slowly walking deeper into a flooded hotel room, water up to her shoulders, calm posture, cream curtains visible in background, soft overcast morning light, muted teal walls, very slow gentle truck out, 35mm cinematic Tarkovsky.`

---

**EDITING NOTES:**
Hold shot 1 for the full 3 seconds before cutting — the stillness sets the tone. Cuts 2 → 3 → 4 should be tight (every 2.5-3s) to build subliminal unease. Hold shot 8 for the final 4 seconds with no cut. Sound design: under shot 1 add a barely-perceptible water-lapping foley; introduce a low-frequency 40Hz drone starting at shot 4. No dialogue. Optional: a single seabird cry between shots 7 and 8.
tips: If you have access to Gen-3 Turbo or Pika 2, regenerate each prompt 3-4 times — AI video models are inconsistent, and you'll pick the best take. For Sora, simplify the prompts (Sora handles motion direction implicitly; over-specifying breaks it).

title: Single-Shot AI Video Prompt Builder for Runway / Pika / Kling
promptText:
Build me a single AI video prompt for [tool] that produces a usable shot on the first try.

TOOL: {Runway Gen-3 / Pika 2 / Kling / Luma Dream Machine}
WHAT I WANT TO SEE (plain English): {your_idea}
MOOD / GENRE: {cinematic / surreal / horror / nature-doc / commercial / anime / etc.}
MOTION I WANT IN THE SHOT: {what_moves — subject, camera, environment, none}
LENGTH: {seconds — usually 4-10}
ASPECT: {16:9 / 9:16 / 1:1}

GENERATE A PROMPT THAT INCLUDES, IN THIS EXACT ORDER:
1. **Subject** (who/what is in frame, with 2-3 specific visual descriptors)
2. **Action** (1 specific motion, written as a verb)
3. **Environment** (where it is — 2 descriptors)
4. **Light** (source, quality, direction — 'overcast morning, soft, from screen-left')
5. **Camera & lens** (35mm, 50mm, 85mm, anamorphic, wide, telephoto)
6. **Camera movement** ('static', 'slow dolly-in', 'handheld', 'truck right')
7. **Mood / color reference** (Tarkovsky, Wong Kar-wai, Roger Deakins, Edward Hopper, A24, 90s VHS, etc.)
8. **Motion qualifiers** ('slow gentle', 'subtle', 'no fast motion')

RULES:
- ≤80 words.
- Don't use 'beautiful', 'amazing', 'stunning'.
- Don't ask for text, faces with specific identities, or copyrighted characters.
- Avoid impossible camera moves (e.g. 360° around a fast-moving object — these break).
- Pick ONE color palette anchor (don't list 5 references — pick 1).

ALSO PROVIDE:
- **What to expect:** 1 line explaining what the tool tends to get RIGHT in this kind of prompt and what it might get WRONG.
- **First retry adjustment:** if the first generation isn't good, what specific word to change.
expectedOutcome:
**TOOL:** Runway Gen-3
**Idea:** A woman runs through a foggy forest at dawn.
**Mood:** Cinematic dreamy, slightly melancholic
**Length:** 6 seconds, 16:9

---

**PROMPT (78 words):**
`A woman in her late 20s wearing a long dark green coat and brown leather boots, dark hair loose, runs steadily through a dense pine forest at dawn, low mist hovering knee-height, cool early morning light filtering through the trees from screen-right, 35mm cinematic, handheld camera following at her hip level slightly behind her, subtle motion blur, muted blue-green color palette in the style of Roger Deakins, slow gentle pace, no fast motion, atmospheric stillness around her movement.`

---

**What to expect:**
Runway Gen-3 is excellent at atmospheric forest + dawn light, and it handles 'handheld following a runner' well at slow paces. It tends to GET WRONG: the boots (often morphs them to wrong shape mid-shot) and the coat color (can drift between green and grey). It tends to GET RIGHT: the mist, the light direction, and the overall film-like grain.

**First retry adjustment:**
If the runner's motion looks robotic or sped-up, change 'runs steadily' to 'jogs slowly' — Runway interprets 'runs' as fast-action and overcompensates with cartoonish gait.
tips: Keep your prompts under 80 words. Beyond that, AI video models start ignoring the back half. Build the prompt in the exact order listed — these tools weight the first 3 elements (subject/action/environment) heaviest.

title: Voiceover Script Built for ElevenLabs / Play.HT (Pause Cues + Emphasis)
promptText:
Convert my raw script into a voiceover-ready script formatted for ElevenLabs / Play.HT / OpenAI TTS so it actually sounds human.

RAW SCRIPT:
```
{paste_your_script}
```

TONE I WANT: {warm_narrator / energetic_explainer / quiet_intimate / authoritative_documentary}
AUDIENCE & USE: {YouTube_explainer / app_onboarding / podcast_intro / audiobook_chapter}
LENGTH I'M TARGETING: {seconds_or_words}

REWRITE THE SCRIPT WITH:
1. **Sentence-level pauses** marked as `<break time="0.5s" />` (ElevenLabs syntax). Pause 0.3-0.6s after declarative sentences, 0.8-1.2s after rhetorical shifts, 1.5s before key reveals.
2. **Emphasis cues** using ALL CAPS for words to stress (1-2 per paragraph max). TTS engines push slight inflection on these.
3. **Sentence length variation.** Mix 5-word sentences with 15-word sentences. AI voices sound robotic on uniform sentence length.
4. **Contractions where natural** ('it is' → 'it's'). TTS handles these better than the long form.
5. **No tongue-twister cluster consonants** ('rugged red roof rebuilds' = avoid). If the original has them, rewrite the line.
6. **Read-the-numbers conversion.** '$1,250' → 'twelve hundred and fifty dollars' OR keep as-is, but pick one and stay consistent.

OUTPUT:
- **Original script length:** X words
- **Voiceover-ready script:** [paste with markup]
- **Estimated duration:** Y seconds at 165 wpm
- **3 lines flagged for re-take:** [lines TTS will likely mispronounce or stumble on]
expectedOutcome:
**Original script length:** 92 words.

**Voiceover-ready script:**

Most people think AWS bills get out of control because of usage. <break time="0.6s" /> They don't.<break time="0.8s" />

They get out of control because of FORGOTTEN resources.<break time="0.5s" /> A test EC2 instance from six months ago.<break time="0.4s" /> An old S3 bucket nobody's touched since 2022. <break time="0.5s" /> Quiet, idle, expensive.<break time="1.0s" />

Last weekend I found four of them. <break time="0.5s" /> Together they were costing me eleven HUNDRED dollars a month.<break time="1.2s" />

So here's what I want to show you. <break time="0.4s" /> An audit you can run in thirty minutes. <break time="0.4s" /> No new tools. No consultants. <break time="1.5s" />

Let's start with the easiest one first.

---

**Estimated duration:** ~42 seconds at 165 wpm.

**3 lines flagged for re-take:**
1. 'eleven HUNDRED' — ElevenLabs occasionally renders this as 'eleven-hundred' compound. If it sounds off, write '$1,100' literally and let the engine decide.
2. 'S3 bucket' — TTS engines pronounce 'S3' as 'es-three' correctly 80% of the time. If wrong, change to 'S-three bucket'.
3. 'six months ago' — slightly mumbled in fast-tempo voices. If using Adam or Bella, add `<break time="0.2s" />` between 'months' and 'ago'.
tips: Don't over-mark pauses. More than ~3 breaks per sentence will make the voice sound mechanical. The natural rhythm comes from contractions + sentence length variation more than explicit pause tags.

title: Reply to a Rude/Aggressive Email Without Losing the Higher Ground
promptText:
Help me reply to a rude or aggressive email professionally. The goal is to defuse, hold my position, and protect the relationship if possible — without rolling over or escalating.

THE EMAIL I RECEIVED (paste it raw, including tone):
```
{paste_the_email}
```

WHO SENT IT: {their_role_and_my_relationship_to_them — boss, client, peer, vendor}
WHAT THEY'RE ACTUALLY UPSET ABOUT (your read): {the_underlying_concern}
MY POSITION (what I actually think): {what_I_believe_is_true}
WHAT I WANT THE OUTCOME TO BE: {keep_relationship? push_back? exit?}
STAKES: {low / medium / high — does this person have power over me?}

WRITE THE REPLY USING THIS STRUCTURE:
1. **Acknowledge the concern** (1 line — names what they're upset about WITHOUT agreeing with their framing).
2. **Take responsibility for what's actually mine** (1-2 lines — be specific).
3. **Hold the line on what's not** (1-2 lines — calm, factual, no emotional language).
4. **Propose the next step** (1 line — concrete action, not 'happy to discuss').
5. **Close warmly** (1 line — no exclamation points, no 'best best best').

RULES:
- No 'sorry you feel that way'. No 'with respect'.
- Don't mirror their tone. The lower-key you sound, the more powerful you read.
- Don't apologize for things you didn't do.
- ≤120 words.
- Skip the salutation if it would feel forced — open directly.

AFTER THE REPLY, give me a 1-line read on the underlying dynamic (what's REALLY going on) so I know what to watch for.
expectedOutcome:
**They sent:** 'This is the 3rd time you've missed the deadline. Frankly I'm questioning whether you can handle this account at all. Need to see real urgency from your team THIS WEEK.'

**Reply:**

Hi James,

I hear you on the urgency, and the timing on the last two deliverables wasn't acceptable.

The first one (the audit) ran late because we expanded scope mid-flight at your team's request — I should have raised the new timeline in writing. That's on me. The most recent deliverable was on time per the revised schedule we agreed in our 9/12 call; I'll resend that thread so we're aligned on dates going forward.

Let's get on a 20-minute call this week to lock the next two milestones and the escalation path if anything slips. I'm proposing Thursday 3pm.

Thanks for the directness.

Maya

---

**Underlying dynamic:** James is probably under heat himself and forwarding pressure down. Your reply gives him something to forward back upstream ('she owned X, here's the next step') — that's why it works without rolling over. Watch for whether he accepts the call. If he won't book it, the real issue isn't this project.
tips: Wait at least 90 minutes before sending. The first draft is for you to vent on paper; the second draft is the one that ships.

title: Follow Up After 7 Days of Silence — 3 Versions
promptText:
I sent an email N days ago and haven't heard back. Help me write a follow-up that doesn't feel pestering and actually gets a reply.

ORIGINAL EMAIL I SENT (paste verbatim):
```
{paste_original}
```

WHEN I SENT IT: {how_many_days_ago}
WHO I SENT IT TO AND OUR RELATIONSHIP: {context}
WHY I THINK THEY MIGHT NOT HAVE REPLIED: {your_honest_guess — busy / not interested / forgot / dragging feet / no internal buy-in}
WHAT I NEED FROM THEM: {the_specific_ask}
HOW BADLY I NEED IT: {nice_to_have / time_sensitive / blocking_me}

GIVE ME 3 FOLLOW-UP OPTIONS:

**Option A — 'Top of inbox' (lightest touch).** 1-2 lines. Resends the ask gently. Best for: they're probably just busy.

**Option B — 'Make it easier' (medium touch).** Restructures the ask as a Yes/No question so it's quicker to reply to. Adds a small new piece of info or context.

**Option C — 'Direct close' (firmest touch).** Names the ambiguity head-on. Offers them an easy 'no' so the thread ends cleanly. Best for: you'd rather have a 'no' than another week of silence.

RULES:
- All 3 options ≤60 words.
- Reply in the same thread (subject: 'Re: original subject') — don't change the subject line.
- Don't apologize for following up.
- Don't use 'just circling back', 'bumping this up', 'gentle nudge'.
- Don't ask if they got the email.

AFTER, tell me which option fits THIS situation best and why.
expectedOutcome:
**Context:** You sent a cold-ish pitch to a head of marketing at a Series B SaaS 8 days ago about a partnership. No reply.

---

**Option A — Top of inbox**

Hi Sara — bringing this back up. Happy to share more on what a 4-week trial would look like, or just to know if this isn't the right fit right now.

Maya

---

**Option B — Make it easier**

Hi Sara — wanted to make this easier to respond to.

Would a 20-min call next Tue or Thu work? If neither — no problem, happy to send a 1-page doc with what I'm proposing and you can decide async.

Maya

---

**Option C — Direct close**

Hi Sara — I don't want to be the person who keeps following up. If this isn't a priority for your team right now, totally fair — just hit reply with a 'not now' and I'll close the loop on my side.

If it is, I'll send a short proposal today.

Maya

---

**Best fit for THIS situation: Option B.**

Cold outreach to a busy head-of role rarely gets reply on a 'top of inbox' nudge — they need a clearer next step. Option C is too strong for a first follow-up; save it for the second one. Option B reduces the cost-of-reply to a Yes/No while still keeping the door open.
tips: If Option B doesn't work in 5 days, send Option C. Don't follow up more than 3 times. The fourth is harassment regardless of how polite the language is.

title: Apology Email to a Customer After a Real Screw-Up
expectedOutcome:
**Subject:** Yesterday's outage — what broke and what we're doing about it

We owe you a real apology.

From 2:14pm to 6:47pm CET yesterday, our document-editor service was down. Customers on the Pro and Team plans couldn't open or save documents during that window. We know this hit you in the middle of a workday and likely cost you real time on real work.

What happened: a routine database migration over the weekend left an indexing job stuck. Under normal load it was invisible. At yesterday's traffic peak it cascaded and brought editing offline. The team rolled back the migration and the service has been stable since 6:47pm.

What we're doing so this doesn't happen again: we've split the migration runner into a separate cluster (so any future stuck job can't take down editing), added a synthetic test that runs the exact failure scenario hourly, and added a public status subscription so you get notified within 60 seconds of any incident.

We've already credited your account for 1 month of your subscription — it'll show up on your next invoice.

This was on us. Thanks for your patience yesterday.

Maya — co-founder
tips: Write this email the SAME DAY the incident happens, not two days later. Speed of response is a bigger trust signal than the polish of the writing.

title: Make a Mutual-Connection Introduction Email (Both People Are Happy)
expectedOutcome:
**Subject:** Priya <> Daniel — quick intro re: onboarding metrics

Hi both,

Making this intro because you've each been thinking hard about the same thing — onboarding activation in B2B SaaS — and would probably learn something from comparing notes.

Priya leads product at Mercer. She rebuilt onboarding there last year and got new-account activation from 22% to 60% in two quarters. She's been writing publicly about how she did it and is currently figuring out how to apply the same playbook to their enterprise tier.

Daniel is the head of growth at Linear-affiliate Stride. He's been running an experimentation system for activation across 4 product squads — has probably the most disciplined A/B testing setup I've seen at company stage. He's been wanting to talk to someone who's done activation-by-segment work.

I'll let you two take it from here. Daniel — can you propose a couple of 20-min slots from your side? Have a good one.

Maya
tips: Always do a DOUBLE OPT-IN before sending — ask both people privately first. Cold intros without consent kill more relationships than they create.

title: Script for Telling Your Manager You're Quitting
promptText:
Help me prepare the conversation where I tell my manager I'm leaving. I want to do this professionally, not torch the relationship, and not give in to any counter-offer pressure.

MY ROLE & MANAGER: {role_and_relationship_quality_with_them}
HOW LONG I'VE BEEN HERE: {tenure}
WHY I'M ACTUALLY LEAVING: {real_reason — be honest, not corporate}
WHAT I'M TELLING THEM (can be different from the real reason): {public_reason}
NOTICE PERIOD I'M OFFERING: {weeks}
WILL I ACCEPT A COUNTER-OFFER UNDER ANY CONDITIONS: {yes/no}
NEW JOB DETAILS (if you want to share or not): {willing_to_share or not}

GIVE ME:

1. **The opening line** — the first 1-2 sentences when you sit down. Direct, no preamble.
2. **The middle** — how to explain the decision in 3 short sentences without going into detail that gives them ammunition to negotiate.
3. **Anticipated objections and the calm response to each:**
   a. 'What can we do to keep you?'
   b. 'Is this about money?'
   c. 'Can you take a week to think about it?'
   d. 'Where are you going?' (if you don't want to share)
   e. 'I'm surprised, this is really bad timing'
4. **The transition wrap-up** — how to redirect the conversation from emotions to practicalities (handover, last day, what's the plan).
5. **The closing line** — how to end the meeting on a good note.

RULES:
- Don't be apologetic. You're not doing anything wrong.
- Don't list grievances. Don't justify.
- Don't say 'I love it here but...' if you don't mean it.
- Don't promise more than you can deliver in the handover.
- Don't agree to a counter-offer in the room, even if it's tempting.
expectedOutcome:
**Opening line (sit down, eye contact, calm voice):**
"I wanted to talk to you in person before anything else — I've accepted another role and I'll be resigning. My last day will be [date], which gives us four weeks."

---

**The middle:**
"This wasn't a fast decision. I've been thinking about it for several months. It comes down to a different kind of work I want to be doing next, and the opportunity came at the right time. It's not a reaction to anything specific here."

---

**Anticipated objections & responses:**

**a. 'What can we do to keep you?'**
"I appreciate you asking, but I've already made the decision and signed. It would be unfair to both sides for me to reopen it."

**b. 'Is this about money?'**
"No, it's not about compensation. It's about the work and the trajectory."

**c. 'Can you take a week to think about it?'**
"I've already taken that time — it's why I waited until now to tell you. I'm here to focus on the handover."

**d. 'Where are you going?'** (if you don't want to share)
"I'd rather hold off on that — happy to share once I've started. What I can say is it's [industry / role type] and it's not a competitor."

**e. 'I'm surprised, this is really bad timing.'**
"I understand. I want to make the handover as clean as possible — let's focus on what would be most useful to you in the next four weeks."

---

**Transition wrap-up:**
"For the handover, I've started writing up the projects I'm currently owning. Can we schedule a 30-min next week to walk through them and decide what gets reassigned vs. wrapped up? I want to leave this clean."

---

**Closing line:**
"I've genuinely valued working with you. I want this last stretch to go well — let's make sure it does."
tips: Have this conversation in the MORNING, not at end of day. They'll need processing time and you'll need to send the formal letter same-day. Bring a single-page transition plan with you — it signals you've thought about them, not just yourself.

title: Birthday Message That Isn't Just 'Happy Birthday!'
expectedOutcome:
**Friend you've known since college, working on a hard career pivot:**

Happy birthday, Daniel.

I still think about that night you spent four hours making my CV not sound like a corporate template — back when neither of us knew what 'PMF' meant and you'd never run a workshop in your life. It's wild to watch you now teach the thing you taught me before you knew you were teaching.

The career bet you're making this year is the right one and it's the hard one. I hope this is the year it pays back what it's cost you. And I hope you remember to take a real day off in it.

Cheers, man.

---

**Coworker you're close with:**

Happy birthday, Priya — hope the cake is real and the meeting at 4pm gets cancelled. Watching you ship that platform redesign without losing the team has been one of the best things to see at work this year. The team's lucky and the calm is contagious.

---

**Parent / family:**

Happy birthday, Mom.

The thing I keep noticing is that you're the only person in our family who actually asks follow-up questions — not the surface ones, the second-tier ones. I think I underestimated how much that shaped how I think about people for most of my life. I'm noticing it more this year.

Thank you for the calls. And the recipes. And the way you laugh.

Love you. Have a soft, slow birthday.
tips: Don't write this as a fill-in-the-blank template. Mention the specific moment. The whole reason a birthday message lands is because the person says 'how the hell did they remember that?'

title: Script the Difficult Conversation Before You Have It
promptText:
I have a difficult conversation coming up. Help me prepare it so I don't blank, escalate, or back down.

WHO IT'S WITH: {role_and_relationship}
WHAT THE TOPIC IS: {the_core_thing}
WHY IT'S DIFFICULT: {power_dynamic / emotional_stakes / fear_of_reaction / unclear_facts}
WHAT I ACTUALLY WANT OUT OF THE CONVERSATION: {your_actual_outcome — what does 'good' look like}
WHAT I'M AFRAID WILL HAPPEN: {the_worst_case_scenario}
WHAT THEY'D PROBABLY SAY (your honest guess): {their_likely_first_response}

GIVE ME:

1. **The opening sentence.** What you say in the first 10 seconds when you sit down. Should orient them to the topic without ambushing them.
2. **Your core point.** 2-3 sentences max. The thing you need them to hear, said simply.
3. **The evidence/specifics.** 2-3 concrete examples that ground the conversation in reality, not feelings.
4. **What you're asking for.** One specific, doable thing. Not 'be different' — something they can actually agree to or decline.
5. **Anticipated reactions + your response:**
   - If they get defensive
   - If they minimize the issue
   - If they go silent / withdraw
   - If they counter-attack ('what about when YOU...')
   - If they agree easily (don't celebrate — clarify the commitment)
6. **Your line in the sand.** What you do if the conversation goes nowhere. Said out loud to yourself, not to them — what's your next move?
7. **The closing.** How to land the conversation. Not 'great talk!' — actually close it.

RULES:
- Use 'I' statements, not 'you always'.
- One topic, one conversation. Don't bundle.
- No 'I just wanted to say...'. Drop 'just'.
- Don't apologize for raising it.
expectedOutcome:
**Context:** Your direct report has been missing standup 2-3x a week. You like them, they're competent on output, but the team is starting to notice.

---

**1. Opening sentence:**
"I want to talk about something that's been on my mind for the last few weeks — your attendance at standup. Mind if we take 15 min?"

**2. Core point:**
"You're missing standup 2-3 times a week. Your work output is great, so the issue isn't performance — but the team is noticing, and it's starting to affect how visible your contributions are."

**3. Evidence:**
- The last 3 weeks: you missed 7 of 14 standups.
- In Slack last Wednesday, Priya asked where the API design RFC was and three other people didn't know it was finished — because you weren't there to flag it.
- Yesterday, two engineers told me they're not sure what you're working on right now.

**4. What I'm asking for:**
"I'd like you to commit to being at standup 4 out of 5 days for the next 4 weeks. If something specific is making it hard — calendar conflict, focus time, anything — I want to know so we can move it. But the default needs to flip."

**5. Anticipated reactions:**

- **Defensive: 'I'm doing great work though — does standup actually matter?'**
  → 'You're right that the work is great. Standup matters because visibility matters. People on the team don't see your work the way I do. I need to fix that.'

- **Minimizing: 'I think I've only missed like 2 or 3.'**
  → 'I checked the data — it's been 7 in the last 3 weeks. I want to make sure we're on the same page about the pattern before we figure out the fix.'

- **Goes silent / withdraws.**
  → Wait. Don't fill the silence. After 5-7 seconds: 'What's coming up for you right now?'

- **Counter-attack: 'Other people miss too — why am I getting this conversation?'**
  → 'Two reasons: it's been the most consistent recently, and you're someone whose work the team should see more of. The other patterns we'll handle separately.'

- **Agrees easily: 'Yeah I'll be there.'**
  → 'Great. Let's make it concrete — does the 9am time still work for you? Anything I should know about your calendar that conflicts?'

**6. Line in the sand (internal — don't say this in the meeting):**
If this conversation doesn't change behavior in 2 weeks, the next conversation moves from 'this matters for visibility' to 'this is now a written goal in your check-in document'. I will not bring this up a third time as a casual ask.

**7. Closing:**
"Thanks for the conversation. Let's check in on this in 2 weeks at our 1:1 — I'll keep an eye on it and bring data, not vibes. Anything else on your mind while we're here?"
tips: Write this out the day BEFORE, sleep on it, edit in the morning. The conversations you over-prepare for tend to go best because you stop being scared of the reactions.

title: 30 Reel/Short Hooks That Stop the Scroll in 1 Second
promptText:
Give me 30 ready-to-record hooks for Instagram Reels / TikTok / YouTube Shorts for my niche. Each hook is the first 1-2 seconds — the line that determines whether someone watches or scrolls.

MY NICHE: {niche}
MY EXPERTISE / ANGLE: {what_makes_you_credible_here}
WHO I'M TALKING TO: {your_ideal_viewer}
MY USUAL TONE: {analytical / contrarian / explanatory / story-driven}

USE THESE 10 HOOK PATTERNS, 3 HOOKS EACH:

1. **Direct address** ('If you're a [niche], stop doing this NOW.')
2. **Shocking number/result** ('I made $X doing Y in 30 days.')
3. **Contrarian** ('Everything you've heard about X is wrong.')
4. **Curiosity gap** ('Nobody talks about X.')
5. **Mistake call-out** ('You're making this [X] mistake without knowing.')
6. **Question hook** ('Why do most [Xs] fail at [Y]?')
7. **Story open** ('I lost $X / a client / a job because of this.')
8. **Comparison** ('I tried [A] vs [B] for 30 days.')
9. **Authority drop** ('A senior [role] explains [thing] in 30 seconds.')
10. **Surprise reveal** ('Watch what happens when I...')

FORMAT EACH HOOK AS:
[Pattern] | [Hook] | [1-line note on what to film visually as you say it]

RULES:
- Each hook ≤12 words.
- No 'Did you know'.
- No 'Today I'm going to show you'.
- Specific over generic — name actual things.
- Hooks should sound like someone talking, not reading.
